prompt:
For each question, decide if it is a **statistical question** (S) or **not** (N). Combine your $4$ answers in order as a string (e.g., $SNSN$):
1) How tall am I?
2) How tall is each player on the team?
3) How tall is the tallest building in Dubai?
4) How many minutes does it take students in my class to eat lunch?
hint: Words such as "each" or "students in my class" signal a group whose answers will vary. A question about one person or one thing has one answer.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Easy ones first: "How tall am I?" has only **one** answer — not statistical. "How tall is each player?" → different heights, so statistical.
Words such as "each" or "students in my class" signal a group whose answers will vary. A question about one person or one thing has one answer.
Label them in order: question 1 is about one person, question 2 about many players, question 3 about one building, and question 4 about many students. Write N for one answer and S for many.
The labels in order are N, S, N, S, so the answer is $NSNS$.

explanation: A statistical question expects variability, so check each question for one answer or many.
1) "How tall am I?" is about one person with one height, so it is **N**.
2) "How tall is each player on the team?" covers many players with different heights, so it is **S**.
3) "How tall is the tallest building in Dubai?" is about one building with one height, so it is **N**.
4) The lunch question covers many students whose times vary, so it is **S**.
Putting the four labels in order gives the answer $NSNS$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Rule of thumb
steps: Singular subject + specific fact = not statistical (one answer).
Group subject + measurable quantity = statistical (many answers, varying).
The words "**each**", "**every**", "**students**", "**players**" almost always signal a statistical question.

alternativeExplanations.title: Could you graph the data?
steps: If you imagined collecting data, would there be a spread to **plot**?
1) Just one height → nothing to spread. N.
2) Heights of many players → dot plot of heights. S.
3) One building's height → no spread. N.
4) Lunchtimes of many students → dot plot of times. S.
